name: The Healthy Pipeline
source: Deal dimensions: Solution Selling-tradition defaults, TO VALIDATE against B2B Klubben course material. Seller craft section added 2026-10: per-meeting skill metrics (Curiosity, Framing), scored per meeting and trended per seller — never merged into deal state.

bands.label: not_addressed
bands.description: Dimension not meaningfully addressed, or no citable evidence exists.

bands.label: touched_unverified
bands.description: Raised in the meeting, but the evidence is seller-assumed; the customer did not confirm it in their own words.

bands.label: established
bands.description: Confirmed by the customer, directly and unambiguously.

bands.label: customer_articulated
bands.description: The customer articulated it unprompted or co-created it; strongest possible evidence.

dimensions.name: Pain
dimensions.definition: The customer has articulated a concrete, admitted business problem in their own words, with consequences.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for the customer describing a problem, its cost, or its consequences themselves. A seller stating the problem and the customer merely agreeing ('yes, exactly') is seller-assumed, not customer-stated. Note euphemistic or hedged Danish phrasing ('det er lidt en udfordring') as weaker evidence than concrete statements with numbers.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'We lose roughly two weeks per project on rework.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'So efficiency is the issue, right?' Customer: 'Mm.'

dimensions.name: Power
dimensions.definition: We know who owns the budget and the decision, and we are either talking to them or have a credible, agreed path to them.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for named roles and people, budget ownership, the decision process, and explicit requests for or grants of access to the economic buyer. A title alone is not power; confirmed decision authority is.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'The final call is mine, and I've set aside budget in Q1.'
dimensions.lowExample: No discussion of who decides or pays; seller assumes the contact person decides.

dimensions.name: Vision
dimensions.definition: The customer holds a concrete vision of solving the problem with our capabilities — ideally one they helped build.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for the customer describing a future state ('if we could X, then we would Y') connected to the seller's offering. Co-creation (customer extends or corrects the how) scores higher than passive acceptance of the seller's pitch.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'So if your model flags the risky projects each Monday, my team could reassign people the same week.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller describes the solution; customer listens without engaging with the how.

dimensions.name: Value
dimensions.definition: The value is quantified and agreed by the customer — the cost of the pain and the worth of solving it — not just claimed by the seller.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for numbers: hours, money, risk, opportunity — and for who states them. Customer-stated or customer-confirmed quantification scores high; seller-claimed ROI with no customer confirmation stays in the unverified band.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'If that saves each PM two hours a week, that is easily half a million kroner a year for us.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'This typically pays for itself in three months.' No customer response.

dimensions.name: Control
dimensions.definition: The seller controls the DEAL process: a clear, mutually agreed next step with owners, dates, and a path to decision.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look at how the meeting ends — but score the deal's forward motion, not meeting hygiene (that is the Framing craft metric). A scheduled next meeting with an agreed purpose, named participants, and dates scores high. 'Send me some material and we'll be in touch' with no commitment scores low. A mutual action plan or agreed decision timeline is the strongest evidence.
dimensions.highExample: Agreed: workshop on the 14th with the CFO present; customer sends current process docs before then.
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'I'll send a proposal.' Customer: 'Great, thanks.' Nothing scheduled.

sellerCraft.note: Per-meeting seller skill, never merged into deal state. Trended per seller across meetings.

bands.label: absent
bands.description: The behavior is essentially missing from the meeting.

bands.label: inconsistent
bands.description: Present in places, skipped in others; shallow where depth was available.

bands.label: deliberate
bands.description: Consistent, intentional practice through the meeting.

bands.label: masterful
bands.description: Systematic and generative: the behavior visibly produces measurable or actionable material.

metrics.name: Curiosity
metrics.definition: The seller asks clarifying questions to statements — staying curious even when the signal seems clear and the intent apparent — because deeper questioning reveals figures, reasoning, or background that is measurable or actionable.
metrics.analysisGuidance: Score exchange pairs: a participant statement and what the seller asked next. High: the seller digs past an apparently clear signal into quantities ('hvor meget tid?'), causes ('hvad skyldes det?'), stakes ('hvad betyder det for jer?') or background — and the digging yields numbers, reasoning or actionable facts. Low: signals accepted at face value, the seller moves on or pitches. Every accepted-at-face-value opening is a MISS: record the customer's verbatim statement and draft the clarifying question the seller could have asked, in the meeting's dominant language, natural and consultative. Do not count rhetorical or leading questions as curiosity.

metrics.name: Framing
metrics.definition: One score, two checkpoints. Opening: the seller deliberately frames the meeting early — intent, purpose and expected outcome of the time spent. Closing (re-framing): toward the end, the seller returns to the frame and evaluates coverage — was everything addressed; which questions remain open; does each open question become an action for a named participant or is it deliberately deferred to the next call.
metrics.analysisGuidance: Check two moments. OPENING (first ~10% of the meeting): is there an explicit statement of why we are here, what we will cover and what a good outcome looks like? Confirmed with the customer ('does that match what you had in mind?') scores higher than announced. CLOSING: does the seller revisit the opening frame, check coverage, and explicitly sort open items into actions-with-owners or deliberate deferrals? A closing that only agrees next steps without revisiting the frame belongs to the Control dimension, not here. Score both checkpoints; one missing caps the combined score at 6. Record a checkpoint entry for each with a verbatim quote when present.
